justification_text:
The point estimates at each forecast horizon (1 day, 1 week, and 1 month) are driven by my expectation of continuity or consistency in the underlying trend or value being modeled. In this scenario, I have assumed that the best guess of the future value, barring significant new information, is the current level or a level influenced by recent observations. Essentially, the point estimate reflects the central tendency of where I expect the value to lie, averaged across my understanding of past performance and present conditions. Over time horizons of 1 day to 1 month, the point estimate remains fixed here at 393.17, suggesting that I have modeled the central expectation of stability in the absence of anticipated major directional movement.

The confidence interval (CI) widths grow wider as the forecast horizon extends due to increasing uncertainty over time. On a 1-day horizon, less time has passed for unpredictable events to occur, so the confidence interval is relatively narrow. For the 1-week and 1-month horizons, the range of possible influences — including market volatility, external shocks, or fundamental changes — grows larger, leading to wider intervals to capture this greater uncertainty. Factors such as random fluctuations, unforeseen events, or compounding variance in processes affecting the forecast add to this. The 90% confidence interval reflects a statistical measure that I have calibrated to represent the range within which I believe the outcome will fall 90% of the time, but with growing time, the unknowns naturally accumulate.

Certain risks or events could push outcomes outside of these stated confidence intervals, especially over longer horizons. Examples might include unexpected economic data releases, geopolitical events causing broader market disruption, policy announcements, or industry-specific developments that could significantly deviate from the trends or relationships I’ve implicitly assumed. Over a 1-month time frame, more dramatic shifts become likelier, as forecasting inherently becomes less precise with more time for systemic shocks or surprises to materialize. Thus, while the intervals aim to account for typical uncertainty, rare or extreme events (sometimes called "black swan" events) could still lie outside this range.
